It replaces the standard linear hemispherical shading $(1 + \mathbf{N} \cdot \mathbf{L})/2$ with a cubic approximation $(1 + \mathbf{N} \cdot \mathbf{L})^3/8$, which culls back-lit surfaces more effectively and reduces erroneous energy on surfaces facing away from the light [S1, unofficial][S2].

The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly states that the standard hemispherical shading operator is $E = (1 + N.L)/2$. It further explains that Scoggins et al. suggested raising this term to the cube to create Gamma-Corrected Hemispherical Shading (GCHS). The text notes that GCHS 'culls back-lit surfaces more effectively' and 'approximates the max operator' (which handles visibility and reduces erroneous energy on back-facing surfaces). Source [S2] confirms the formula for the cubic approximation as $(1 + N.L)^3/8$ (derived from $((1+N.L)/2)^3$) and states that an exponent of 3 is optimal for producing an inflection point to pass through 0 and 1, minimizing error. Both sources support the claim that the cubic approximation replaces the linear hemispherical shading to better cull back-lit surfaces and reduce erroneous energy.
